strengths: The paper is well motivated and easy to follow.
Comparisons against the baseline and also early-stopping / data-efficiency methods show strong SOTA in training acceleration for a few datasets.
The speedups are not just in nominal sample complexity, but also in world-clock training time.
The method only relies on the forward path and has an efficient implementation path in most ML frameworks.
The paper is well-written, presents an interesting and intuitive idea, and is well-positioned within the existing literature.
The proposed early stopping criterion offers computational efficiency by avoiding back-propagation, leading to faster training and reduced computation without sacrificing generalization.
The empirical results are extensive and address critical questions related to the method's effectiveness.
The idea is simple, intuitive and provides a very elegant in-between to curriculum learning, dynamic data pruning and early stopping.
The flow of the paper is very good, and the literature review feels very strong (only with some minor issues in relation to dynamic data pruning that I mention later).
The experiments are well thought through and feel reasonably extensive.
The results are great, which is a very good sign for a methodology paper.
It will be of interest to the research community, especially due to connection to various research fields mentioned in Section 2, and clear improvements to a very popular algorithm (early stopping).
The authors explicitly pointed out their lack of studies on underrepresented groups in the Limitations, clearly opening a path for future research.
weaknesses: There is no theoretical analysis of the proposed method presented. There is also no rigorous suggestion on how one might attempt such analysis.

There is no mention of catastrophic forgetting, which is a well-known and well-studied topic in non-uniform training (e.g. in RL and active learning). This setup is not as episodic as a full-blown RL domain, but there are clear similarities that would suggest catastrophic forgetting could occur if examples are completely dropped (too early) and never revisited. I suggest adding at least one experiment in which early dropped examples are evaluated at the end of training to measure and report any forgetting effects.

The empirical test cases are very limited. SOTA results only on CIFAR-10/100 are not enough to establish the efficacy of the method on other settings. The study on the higher level (yet still vision) tasks is also somewhat limited and not against other data-efficiency methods. A comparison vs. other method can be added to the higher-level vision task study to improve the analysis.

Instance-based early stopping can introduce biases in the learning process that affect fairness or policy considerations. Without special care such side effects are bound to happen. To study this effect, one could build an adversarial dataset with easy examples from one protected group and harder ones from another group; non-uniform training can result in shifted per-group precision/recall metrics compared to the baseline, which can be measured and reported.

A crucial missing element in this study is an analysis of the impact of noisy samples within the training set. It is likely that in the presence of noisy labels, correctly labeled samples would be quickly learned and excluded, leaving the model to train primarily on incorrect information, potentially causing the model to "forget" previously learned correct trends and suffer from significantly worse generalization performance compared to standard training. A corresponding analysis for noisy datasets is crucial to fully evaluate the robustness and practicality of the proposed method.

The "mastered" criterion introduces two new hyperparameters: a threshold (delta) and a step count (N). Introducing additional hyperparameters necessitates further tuning and selection, which reduces the practicality of the method. It remains unclear how to optimally select them for datasets significantly different in nature from CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, raising concerns about the method's generalizability and ease of use across diverse datasets.

The claim that the second-order difference removal criterion has been extensively validated is too strong; more thorough analysis of higher-order loss information (e.g., third-order) and trade‑offs between computational cost and performance gains is needed.

The authors did not include training times in Figure 5 and only compared with one dynamic data pruning method; a more comprehensive comparison—including additional dynamic data pruning techniques and training‑time measurements—is needed to fully assess how IES compares in terms of computational overhead and convergence behavior.
Equation 2 should explicitly state that the formula comes from a Taylor approximation and explain how the second‑order difference relates to the curvature of the loss function.
It is not clear why different optimizers were used for different architectures; a justification or reference is needed because optimizer choice can significantly impact performance.
Typos are present in lines L137, L328, L368, L423, and L1004.

The statement in L295‑L296 that the method can reduce the number of training instances in backpropagation by over 40% should specify that this reduction occurs only in the later stages of training; otherwise it is ambiguous and could be considered overselling.

The experiments do not fully explore the performance of IES under different computational constraints; it would be valuable to compare across different speedups (e.g., Table 4) to see how effectiveness scales with varying speedup levels.
